stories.body: Russia launched a major missile attack on Kyiv and other Ukrainian regions hours after Vladimir Putin told US envoy Steve Witkoff that Moscow was prepared in principle to resume trilateral talks with the United States and Ukraine after 10 November. At least two people were killed and 22 wounded in Kyiv, where strikes damaged homes, energy infrastructure, a bridge, an ambulance station and other civilian sites; Odesa's port was also hit. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the attack showed Russia had not changed its approach to the war and called for more air defences, Patriot interceptors and sanctions, while Ukraine's foreign minister said flattery and appeasement would not stop Russian aggression.
stories.headline: Russia strikes Kyiv hours after signalling readiness to resume Ukraine peace talks

stories.body: Houthi drone and missile attacks killed two people at King Fahd International Airport in Dammam and two more when debris from an intercepted drone fell near an Aramco oil facility, Saudi authorities said. The Houthis also claimed attacks against Saudi defence and energy targets, while the United States ordered some diplomats and family members to leave Saudi Arabia because of attacks on civilian airports and critical infrastructure. The violence, along with reported Iranian attacks on vessels and mines near the Strait of Hormuz, pushed Brent crude above $112 a barrel as markets feared further disruption to global oil supply.
stories.headline: Houthi attacks kill civilians in Saudi Arabia as regional conflict threatens oil supplies

stories.body: Iran's Revolutionary Guard says it has shifted from a defensive posture to an offensive and asymmetric doctrine, warning that a new attack could bring retaliation as well as operations against countries hosting US military bases. The announcement came amid continuing attacks on shipping around the Strait of Hormuz, Houthi strikes in Saudi Arabia and reports that the US and Israel are considering further attacks on Iran after the US midterm elections. President Donald Trump denied that negotiations with Tehran were under way but said the conflict could be resolved fairly soon; Iran says its missile stockpile and capabilities have expanded since the 2025 war.
stories.headline: Iran adopts an offensive military doctrine as Trump hints at possible action

stories.body: Authorities, companies and website operators are rushing to patch security flaws in PHP, the programming language used by roughly 70% of websites. Researchers say the vulnerabilities had existed for years and may be difficult for people to exploit, but artificial intelligence could make exploitation much easier; major security companies have already recorded millions of attempted attacks. No successful breach linked to the flaws has yet been publicly confirmed, but the disclosure of the bugs before patching was complete has created an urgent race between defenders and attackers, especially because older PHP installations may need upgrading before they can apply the fix.
stories.headline: Governments race to patch serious PHP vulnerabilities affecting millions of websites

stories.body: President Emmanuel Macron said only demonstrations organised by authorised unions would be permitted in many French cities this weekend after protests over living costs and school conditions were followed by rioting, looting and damage to businesses and historic buildings. Cities including Lyon and Nice have imposed broader bans, while police deployments will rise by 20%. Authorities say about 2,700 people were arrested during last weekend's disorder and more than 1,000 have appeared in court, with fast-track proceedings drawing criticism from lawyers who say overwhelmed courts leave too little time to prepare cases.
stories.headline: France limits weekend protests to authorised union demonstrations after violent unrest

stories.body: France has reported the first documented human infection with Shamonda virus, a livestock virus transmitted by biting midges that has been found in cattle, sheep, goats and other animals. The patient, who had a severely weakened immune system, died this month, and investigators are examining whether the infection caused or contributed to neurological complications and how it was acquired. French and European health authorities say the case appears exceptional, with no evidence of sustained human-to-human transmission and no identified risk to the general public, though further surveillance and research are under way.
stories.headline: France reports first known human Shamonda virus infection, with no wider public-health risk identified

stories.body: Wedgewood Polls admitted it fabricated its survey data after an investigation by polling outlet FiftyPlusOne, raising questions about how bogus polls were used by campaigns, donors, media aggregators and prediction markets. Its results had been included by major aggregators and circulated in political coverage, and candidates said they had real consequences: former Michigan Senate candidate Mallory McMorrow said a false poll showing her support collapsing damaged fundraising and volunteer morale. FiftyPlusOne says it had vetted the firm's stated methodology and founders but was misled by fraudulent raw data, highlighting the vulnerability of election coverage to unverified polling.
stories.headline: Fake polling firm may have influenced campaign narratives and fundraising in the 2026 elections

stories.body: Republicans have spent about $677 million on broadcast advertising in 10 key Senate battlegrounds, compared with $479 million for Democrats, but their dependence on outside groups means their money buys less airtime. Candidates and party committees can receive lower broadcast rates, while super PACs pay more, allowing strongly funded Democratic candidates to remain competitive despite a Republican advantage in outside spending. In states including Ohio, Texas and Michigan, the GOP's dollar advantage translates into only a modest majority of ads on air; Republican strategists also say some late ad purchases made by MAGA Inc. increased costs further.
stories.headline: Republicans' Senate spending edge buys fewer television ads than expected

stories.body: Georgia Republicans are relying on billionaire healthcare executive Rick Jackson, who has spent nearly $200 million on his gubernatorial campaign, to prevent a broader Democratic sweep in the state. Jackson remains in a close race with Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms while Republicans fear their Senate candidate, Mike Collins, is falling behind Senator Jon Ossoff and other statewide contests may also be vulnerable. GOP strategists say Jackson has tried to focus on Georgia issues and associate himself with outgoing Governor Brian Kemp rather than Donald Trump, whose visits they worry could energise Democratic voters and alienate undecided moderates.
stories.headline: Georgia Republicans look to self-funding governor candidate Rick Jackson to limit wider losses

stories.body: Spain's conservative Popular Party has released an AI-generated campaign video that imitates the images and voices of socialist politicians and figures close to the government, making them appear to admit wrongdoing. The video, titled "Leftists and Proud," was a response to a real PSOE video in which Pedro Sánchez embraced the label "left-wing" after Argentine President Javier Milei's visit. The PP's video depicts figures including Begoña Gómez, José Luis Ábalos, José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero and Santos Cerdán, prompting the PSOE to condemn the tactic as another step in a campaign based on personal attacks and misinformation.
stories.headline: Spain's PP uses AI-generated videos impersonating socialist figures in escalating campaign tactic

stories.body: Argentine President Javier Milei's visit to Madrid has become a flashpoint in Spain's pre-election campaign after he called Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez an "unpresentable dictator" and embraced Madrid regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso. Sánchez's Socialist Party used the visit to rally its supporters, while the national leadership of the Popular Party sought to avoid making Milei central to the campaign, arguing that the PSOE was using the dispute to distract from domestic concerns. Some PP figures acknowledge that Milei's rhetoric could mobilise progressive voters, even as others praise or defend his political message.
stories.headline: Javier Milei's Madrid visit injects new tension into Spain's election campaign

stories.body: Spain and Italy have agreed not to extend reciprocal border controls on flights and passenger sea connections that were introduced in August after thousands of migrants entered Ceuta from Morocco. Italy initially imposed the checks on travellers arriving from Spain, and Madrid responded with equivalent controls on travellers from Italy. Following talks between the two countries' interior ministers and earlier discussions between Pedro Sánchez and Giorgia Meloni, the governments said the controls would end and be replaced by stronger information-sharing to protect the Schengen area.
stories.headline: Spain and Italy agree to lift border controls imposed during the Ceuta migration crisis

stories.body: Spanish National Police found 74 undocumented migrants, including 10 unaccompanied minors, living in overcrowded and unsanitary conditions in an apartment in Ceuta's El Príncipe neighbourhood. Officers arrested a local man suspected of leading a criminal network that allegedly held migrants while arranging irregular transfers to mainland Spain and may have exploited adults and children for labour. Police said some minors had suffered physical abuse, including dog bites, and the investigation involves alleged offences relating to irregular migration, labour rights, injuries and child labour exploitation.
stories.headline: Police find 74 migrants, including 10 children, crowded into a Ceuta apartment

stories.body: The Popular Party has named Cayetana Álvarez de Toledo and Borja Sémper as second and third, respectively, on Alberto Núñez Feijóo's Madrid list for the 29 November general election. The pairing brings together two prominent but distinct currents within the party: Álvarez de Toledo is seen as a harder-line figure who may appeal to voters near Vox, while Sémper is associated with a more centrist profile. The PP described the list as evidence that it can accommodate different political sensibilities while presenting a broad alternative to the Sánchez government.
stories.headline: Spain's PP places Cayetana Álvarez de Toledo and Borja Sémper behind Feijóo on its Madrid ticket

stories.body: The Spanish and Catalan governments say they will take another formal step next week toward transferring the R1 commuter rail line, which runs from Barcelona through the Maresme to Maçanet-Massanes, to Catalonia. Transport Minister Óscar Puente called the transfer irreversible and said a new Renfe service contract worth about €460 million annually would be approved on Tuesday, alongside Catalan government approval. Both sides are trying to complete the R1 arrangement before Spain's 29 November election, amid concern that a change in national government could complicate pending Rodalies transfers and financing.
stories.headline: Catalonia and Spain say the Rodalies R1 transfer agreement will be signed next week

stories.body: Social organisations in Catalonia are calling on authorities to guarantee accessible, safe and nearby shelter for people living on the streets, in vehicles, settlements or shacks during heavy-rain and other severe-weather alerts. A coalition of homelessness and harm-reduction groups says emergency advice to stay indoors exposes the inequality faced by people without housing, estimating that nearly 24,000 people in Catalonia are homeless. They want emergency accommodation without barriers related to documentation, pets or personal belongings and greater involvement of outreach and homelessness teams in civil-protection planning; nearly 200 unhoused people used emergency accommodation in Barcelona during October's storms.
stories.headline: Social groups demand equal weather-emergency protection for Barcelona's unhoused residents

stories.body: Barcelona contains 32 of Spain's 100 areas with the highest average rents, according to National Statistics Institute data for 2024, led by Pedralbes at €2,002 a month, second only to Madrid's Recoletos. Separate analysis finds that Barcelona households spend an average 35.3% of their income on rent and utilities, above the commonly used 30% affordability threshold, with major differences between districts. In Ciutat Vella, housing-related costs consume 47.4% of average household income, while in Sarrià-Sant Gervasi they account for 26.6%, underscoring persistent inequalities despite rent controls introduced in 2024.
stories.headline: Barcelona's rental burden remains among Spain's highest
